owner_name: The Wider Interests of Football Ltd (Dons Trust subsidiary that owns AFC Wimbledon)
note: The club group bought the former greyhound stadium site from Merton Council in 2019 and opened the new Plough Lane in 2020; the freehold sits in a Dons Trust subsidiary in the same group as the club.

owner_name: London Borough of Waltham Forest (freehold); Matchroom Sport / Barry Hearn holds the long lease
lease_note: Matchroom holds the ~990-year headlease bought in 2008-09 and sub-lets the stadium to the club on a shorter lease
note: Waltham Forest owns the freehold; Barry Hearn's Matchroom bought the long lease in 2008-09 and kept the stadium when the club was sold in 2017 and again to GSG LOFC in 2025. The club plans a new stadium by 2031.

owner_name: Redwood Holdings 1 Ltd (Rob Couhig / Dogwood Football), owner of Reading FC
note: Dai Yongge sold the stadium to his own company Prestige Fortune Asia in 2017-18, separating it from the club; the May 2025 Redwood Holdings takeover bought the club together with the stadium and Bearwood training ground. Whether the stadium now sits in the club company or a sister company in the Redwood group is not confirmed.

owner_name: Frank Adams Legacy Ltd (Wycombe Wanderers Trust)
lease_note: 50-year lease granted to the club when Rob Couhig bought 75% in 2020
note: The supporters' trust put Adams Park into Frank Adams Legacy Ltd in 2012; it kept the ground when it sold control of the club to Rob Couhig in 2020 and the club took a 50-year lease. No source found that the later Mike Dunn takeover changed the ground's ownership.

lease_note: Lease from the council, agreed 2010
note: The council built the stadium and the club has leased it since moving in 1997.

owner_name: Priestfield Developments Ltd (controlled by Brad Galinson)
note: Paul Scally's separate company Priestfield Developments bought the ground in 2007 for £9.8m during a debt restructuring; control of it passed to Brad Galinson in December 2022 alongside his takeover of the club.

The club bought the Guest and Chrimes foundry site in 2010 and opened the stadium in 2012, funded by chairman Tony Stewart. Sources describe it as club-owned; no source found for a separate Stewart company holding.

The club bought the freehold for £7,500 in 1921. Mark and Nicola Palios have controlled the club since 2014, with Indonesia's Santini Group a minority shareholder since 2019; no source found that the ground was moved out of the club.

The stadium opened in 2020 as part of The Quadrant development delivered by Chestnut Homes, the housebuilder owned by club chairman David Newton. Two searches did not establish whether the freehold sits with the club, Chestnut Homes or another body.

Dale Vince's Ecotricity is the named developer of the planned Eco Park stadium and of the plan to replace the New Lawn with 95 homes. Three searches did not establish whether the New Lawn freehold sits with the club or with Ecotricity/Vince.

lease_note: Lease to Hornchurch Football Club (2005) Ltd; council rent review effective 1 June 2025
note: Council-owned athletics and football stadium on Bridge Avenue, Upminster, leased to the club; Havering's 2025 rent review decision confirms the tenancy.

owner_name: Ron Martin / Martin family companies (former club owner)
note: Ron Martin separated Roots Hall from the club during his ownership; when COSU (Justin Rees) bought the club in July 2024 the Martin family kept the ground, with its return tied to a council-brokered deal and Fossetts Farm housing. No source found confirming the ground has since passed back to the club.

lease_note: 140-year lease of the whole ground granted 2020 at peppercorn rent
note: The council owns the ground; in 2020 it granted the club a single 140-year lease of the entire stadium after Telford College gave up its West Stand lease.
The club has played at St James Park, Churchill Way, since 1974. A ground directory lists the club as owner, but no primary source confirming a freehold title was found.
The club has played at The Meadow, Amy Lane, since 1917. Two searches did not establish who holds the freehold.

lease_note: Groundshare licence/lease from Darlington RFC, in place since 2016
note: Darlington FC returned to the town in 2016 as a groundsharing tenant of Darlington RFC, which built Blackwell Meadows in 1994. Council papers show Darlington Borough Council leasing pitch land at the site to the rugby club, so the council may hold some or all of the underlying freehold.

lease_note: Lease surrendered and regranted in 2016, with groundsharing terms carried forward
note: The club leases the Memorial Ground, West Street, from Waverley Borough Council; the 2009 lease was surrendered and replaced by a new lease in 2016.
sources: https://modgov.waverley.gov.uk/documents/s10922/Farnham Town Football Club - Surrender and Regrant of Lease.pdf

ground: Hebburn Sports & Social Ground (Trustmark Group Stadium)
lease_note: Council leases the ground to Hebburn Sports and Social Club, of which the football club is a section
note: South Tyneside Council bought the sports ground in 1982 and leases it to the multi-sport Hebburn Sports and Social Club; it was renamed the Trustmark Group Stadium in August 2025.
After losing Queen Street in 2008 the club bought land at Hop Oast next to Horsham Golf & Fitness, funded by selling land at the Holbrook Club to Croudace Homes, and opened its new ground in 2019.

owner_name: Maidstone United Ground Ltd (Terry Casey and Oliver Ash)
note: Owners Terry Casey and Oliver Ash bought the freehold from the MoD and opened the stadium in 2012. A ground company is listed as owner, and the owners have said they could sell the club while keeping the freehold, which suggests the ground sits outside the club company; a proposed sale to Alan Manchett fell through.

ground: Court Place Farm, Marsh Lane (RAW Charging Stadium)
lease_note: Lease of the football ground from the council
note: The club has played at Court Place Farm since 1993 on council-owned land; council papers from 2008 describe the site as council-owned with a lease to the club, and a 2017 partnership added Oxford United's use of the stadium.
sources: https://mycouncil.oxford.gov.uk/Data/City Executive Board (became Cabinet on 13 May 2019)/200811261700/Agenda/78791Item20.pdf

lease_note: Revised 50-year lease to May 2074, with the club taking over management of the stadium
note: The council built Arbour Park, home since 2016 after 14 homeless years; in 2024 the club secured a new 50-year lease and took over running the venue.

owner_name: Local council (Durham County Council or Spennymoor Town Council - not confirmed which)
lease_note: 25-year lease agreed 25 September 2007
note: The council evicted the previous club from the ground in 2007, then agreed a new 25-year lease. Sources do not say which council holds the freehold.
The council built the sports hub next to the Xcel Leisure Centre, funded by selling the old Stompond Lane ground, for Walton & Hersham and Walton Casuals; it is run by Places Leisure for the council.
The council provided the ground in 1959; the club later bought the freehold from its landlord, Amber Valley Borough Council, after lengthy negotiations.

lease_note: 30-year lease signed after four and a half years of talks, running to 2049
note: The club leases Hurst Cross from Tameside council; a new 30-year lease secured the ground to 2049.

owner_name: Tilstone Holding Ltd (subsidiary of Warehouse REIT)
lease_note: Rolling twelve-month lease for many years
note: The club has played at Station Approach since 1934 on rolling annual leases from a property company; talks on a sale or long lease were paused in 2025 when the landlord's parent, Warehouse REIT, became subject to a takeover.
The club sold its Rhodes Avenue ground for housing in the mid-1990s and moved to the new Woodside Park in 1999. Three searches did not establish who holds the freehold.

lease_note: Historically only five-year leases because the site was earmarked for housing; club sought a longer lease
note: The club moved to Leylands Park in 1969 with Burgess Hill Town Council's help; Mid Sussex District Council is the landlord. Current lease length not confirmed.
Medway Council lists the Maidstone Road Sports Ground in its directory and sources describe the ground as council-owned; it was originally private land owned by George Winch.

lease_note: Club is a tenant; 2017-18 Wiltshire Council papers refer to a new lease from its landlord or a possible purchase
note: Wiltshire Council papers show the club leases its ground from a landlord they do not name (Wiltshire owns only adjacent car-park land, transferred to the club in 2017-18), and mention a possible purchase of the ground. Three searches did not identify the landlord.

lease_note: Long lease of the whole facility at £1 a year rent
note: The council built the £6.5m community stadium, opened in 2006, and owns it; from 2008 it handed management to the club, which leases the whole site for £1 a year.

owner_name: Bishop's Stortford FC (host club; freehold holder not established)
lease_note: Groundshare tenant
note: Enfield FC has no ground of its own; after groundsharing at Hertford Town's council-owned Hertingfordbury Park, it groundshared at Bishop's Stortford's Woodside Park in 2025-26. The file's ground (Hertingfordbury Park) appears out of date, and the 2026-27 arrangement was not confirmed.
The Northolme is owned by the Gainsborough Trinity Supporters' Club, a body separate from the football club company.

owner_name: The James Grove Recreation and Sports Ground Trust (registered charity 515715)
note: The ground, home since 1882, is held by a charitable trust for the use of the people of Halesowen in perpetuity; the club is its occupier.

lease_note: Lease is held by a private company rather than the football club; the trust may lease only to a charitable body
note: A charitable trust set up in 1880 owns Top Field and cannot sell it; the lease sits with a private company, not the club. Club and trust have since announced joint work on the site's future.
A council planning report states the Giant Axe land is owned by the city council and doubles as a public recreation ground used by the club, its home since 1911.
sources: https://committeeadmin.lancaster.gov.uk/(S(uufhck45vr5ey455phwmut55))/documents/s80684/Lancaster City FC The Giant Axe West Road Lancaster.pdf

note: Garretts bought the ground in 1921 for its works athletic association, later renamed Leiston Town Athletic Association; the stadium address is given as the association's, with the football club using it. Whether the association holds the freehold outright was not confirmed.
The club bought the land for Bloomfields with a bequest from former player Arthur Rodwell plus a Lottery grant, and owns the facility.
The club sold its Warwick Avenue ground to the Abbeyfield housing association and moved to Farley Way in 1994. Three searches did not establish who holds the Farley Way freehold.

The club moved from Middlesbrough and settled at Green Lane with the help of the local authority, which suggests council land, but three searches did not confirm who holds the freehold or the lease terms.

owner_name: St Albans City & District Council (held under a trust)
lease_note: Licence, historically renewed at a peppercorn fee, rather than a long lease
note: The council owns Clarence Park, held under a trust, and lets the stadium area to the club on a licence; the club has played there since 1908. The council's Clarence Park forum still met in June 2025.

owner_name: Warwickshire County Council (freehold); leased via Stratford-on-Avon District Council
lease_note: County council agreed in principle (2005) to lease the site to the district council, to be sub-let to the club
note: The club moved to Knights Lane, Tiddington, in 2007-08 on county-council land identified with the district council; the final lease terms were not found. FC Stratford groundshares there.

The club has played at the Rylands Recreation Club ground, opened by the Rylands wireworks for its staff, since 1906; who now holds the freehold was not found. The club says it has secured land for a new stadium, possibly at Crab Lane, Padgate.

ground: The Enclosed Ground, East Brighton Park
note: Brighton Corporation let the club enclose a pitch in the council's East Brighton Park in 1954-55; it remains the home ground. Current lease terms were not found.

ground: Derwent Park (groundshare with Workington Town RLFC while Borough Park is rebuilt)
lease_note: Club surrendered its long lease of Borough Park to the council for the Cumberland Sports Village project
note: Cumberland Council owns Borough Park and Derwent Park; the club gave up its Borough Park lease so the council can build the £16m Cumberland Sports Village there (demolition from May 2026, due summer 2027) and moved to Derwent Park in early 2026.
